justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across all three horizons, starting near 1102 for the one-day forecast and gradually rising to 1120 at one month. This trajectory was driven primarily by the assumption of mean-reverting behavior around a slight positive trend, consistent with how many financial or index-type series behave over short to medium horizons. The one-day estimate anchors closely to the most recent observed value, with only marginal adjustment for expected drift. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, I incorporated a small positive trend component while acknowledging that compounding uncertainty pulls the distribution wider without dramatically shifting the central expectation. In essence, I expected the series to continue doing roughly what it has been doing, just with increasing ambiguity about the exact path.

The confidence interval widths reflect the natural scaling of uncertainty with time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 75 points, which is relatively tight and reflects short-term autocorrelation and low immediate volatility in the series. By one week, that span grows to about 135 points, and at one month it widens to roughly 285 points. This fanning-out pattern follows the square-root-of-time heuristic common in financial forecasting, where volatility accumulates proportionally to the square root of elapsed time. I also factored in that longer horizons are more susceptible to structural breaks, regime changes, and macro shocks that are essentially invisible at the one-day scale but become increasingly plausible over weeks.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include sudden macroeconomic announcements such as central bank rate decisions or inflation surprises, which can cause discontinuous jumps that a smooth trend model would not anticipate. Geopolitical events or financial contagion from other markets could similarly produce tail moves well beyond the 90% bands. On the downside, a sharp risk-off episode or liquidity event could push the series below 1000, outside my lower bound at the monthly horizon. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst — unexpected earnings, policy easing, or a resolution of an ongoing uncertainty — could push above 1265.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly stationary volatility, which is itself an assumption that can break down. If realized volatility were to spike — as it does during crises — the true 90% interval could be considerably wider than what I stated, meaning my confidence bands should be treated as a baseline under normal conditions rather than a hard probabilistic guarantee under all possible environments.
